groups.instruction:
Questions 36-40

Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

In boxes 36-40 on your answer sheet, write

YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.explanation: Answer: FALSE Paragraph 1: ' Many factors lie behind these changes , from the loss of hedgerows to the use of pesticides'.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 2: chicks are fed on caterpillars, and ' caterpillar numbers reach their peak for only two or three weeks in late spring'.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 2: 'mismatch' describes what happens ' when the timing of a bird's breeding no longer coincides with the peak in its food supply ', not a problem with nest sites.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 3 says caterpillars 'have been emerging earlier', but nothing is said about their size.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 4: ' thousands of volunteers also check nests ... creating a record that professional scientists alone could never have produced'.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 5: great tits now lay about two weeks earlier, and ' for the most part they have kept pace with the earlier caterpillar peak '.
Answer: resident Paragraph 5: 'The great tit is a resident species that spends the whole year in Britain'.
Answer: weeks Paragraph 5: great tits 'now lay their eggs about two weeks earlier'.
Answer: Africa Paragraph 6: 'The pied flycatcher spends the winter in West Africa '.
Answer: day Paragraph 6: its journey is 'controlled largely by the length of the day in Africa, which is not affected by climate change'.
Answer: satellite Paragraph 7: 'scientists have fitted cuckoos with tiny satellite tags'.
Answer: heathland Paragraph 8: the Dartford warbler is 'a small bird that lives on heathland in southern England'.
Answer: winters Paragraph 8: 'A series of milder winters has since allowed it to recover and spread much further north'.
Answer: C Paragraph C: lithium is used ' above all in electric vehicles, whose rapidly growing sales have caused demand for the metal to soar '.
Answer: F Paragraph F: ' The largest of these salt flats covers more than ten thousand square kilometres '.

Answer: E Paragraph E explains the formation: ' rain and melting snow have carried dissolved minerals down from the surrounding volcanic mountains into these basins ', the water evaporates, and lagoons at the edges support microbes, insects and flamingos.
Answer: D Paragraph D: the three countries 'have very different laws, and there is no shared agreement on how the resource should be managed '.
Answer: D (Martín Keller) Paragraph F: ' Using brine makes far more sense than continuing to dig enormous open-pit mines on land. '
Answer: B (Quispe, Herrera and Ford) Paragraph D: the paper describes ' the same failure to respect the rights of indigenous communities '.
Answer: A (Paula Ríos) Paragraph B: ' the knowledge locked in these ecosystems may prove to be worth far more than the metal '.
Answer: E (Sofía Mendes) Paragraph F: ' Large-scale pumping will be the most serious threat these birds have ever faced as a result of human activity '.
Answer: B (Quispe, Herrera and Ford) Paragraph D: they warn that ' far too little is known about the underground water systems '.
Answer: C (Tomás Vidal) Paragraph E: ' everyone I work with agrees that there should be no pumping close to the lagoons '.
Answer: ponds Paragraph C: 'Companies pump the brine to the surface and into vast artificial ponds , where the sun gradually evaporates the water'.
Answer: energy Paragraph C: 'Producers argue that this method uses far less energy than extracting lithium from hard rock.'
Answer: water Paragraph C: critics point out that 'it consumes enormous amounts of water in one of the driest regions on the planet'.

text.en: comparing two different theories about human evolution
explaining why he dislikes going to the gym
outlining a common belief about human activity
criticising people who do not exercise enough

questions.explanation: Answer: C The paragraph opens ' It is widely assumed that human beings were designed by evolution to be constantly on the move' and goes on to describe this view. The writer later rejects it, so he is not criticising inactive people (D).

text.en: It was based on careful scientific research.
It reflected the values that were common at that time.
It changed the way that people viewed their ancestors.

questions.explanation: Answer: C ' It fitted well with the spirit of the time , which placed great emphasis on individual responsibility and self-improvement.' The claims came from 'popular books', not careful research (A).

text.en: They are less active than people used to believe.
Their days include long periods of rest as well as activity.
They are unwilling to take part in scientific studies.
Their way of life is changing as a result of modern technology.

questions.explanation: Answer: B The Hadza were 'far more physically active' than office workers, ' Yet they also spent a surprisingly large part of each day resting '.

text.en: doing physical exercise for its own sake is not a traditional human behaviour.
hunter-gatherers are healthier than people in modern societies.
few traditional communities still live by hunting and gathering.
people in traditional communities rarely work hard.

questions.explanation: Answer: A ' Nobody ever went for a run or did physical exercise for its own sake ', and his hosts found the idea of jogging absurd. People did work hard when needed (D).
Answer: active Paragraph 4: they 'were far more physically active than the average office worker'.
Answer: resting Paragraph 4: 'they also spent a surprisingly large part of each day resting , often several hours, sitting in the shade'. 'sitting' is also accepted.
Answer: kneeling Paragraph 6: 'they tend to rest in positions such as squatting and kneeling '.
Answer: muscles Paragraph 6: these positions 'keep the leg muscles working at a low level'.
Answer: calories Paragraph 6: the number of calories the Hadza burned in a day was 'roughly the same as for office workers in industrialised countries'.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writer describes how his hosts spent their time and what they thought of jogging, but never compares their health with that of the Hadza.
Answer: NO Paragraph 7: ' Individuals who used up energy without good reason would have been at a disadvantage. '
Answer: YES Paragraph 8: ' The desire to avoid unnecessary effort is a perfectly natural part of being human '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 9 explains how modern life has removed the need to move, but the writer does not compare people in rural and urban areas.
Answer: NO Paragraph 10: ' simply telling people to try harder is unlikely to work '; campaigns based on that message 'have achieved disappointingly little'.
